Mar

/mahr/ — rhymes with car · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To mar is to impair the appearance of.

Mar — no source sentence supplied.

Worked Example

A luthier spends months restoring an antique violin until the varnish glows like honey. On the morning of the auction, a careless mover drags a metal buckle across the instrument's face, leaving a long white scratch through the finish.

The violin still plays perfectly — only its beauty has been spoiled, and that spoiling of appearance is exactly what mar means. Because the harm is to how something looks rather than how it works, mar is more precise than the generic word 'damage.'

How Strong Is It? — smudge → blemish → ruin → mar

smudge vs. mar

smudge vs. mar: A smudge is weaker than mar — a smudge leaves only a faint mark you can wipe away, while to mar something is to damage its appearance noticeably.

blemish vs. mar

blemish vs. mar: To blemish is slightly weaker than to mar; a blemish is one small flaw, but marring suggests damage that spoils the overall look of the whole thing.

ruin vs. mar

ruin vs. mar: Ruin is stronger than mar — a marred surface is still usable despite its flaws, but a ruined one is damaged beyond repair.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — mar

root — mar: to spoil, damage, or hinder (Old English (merran))

Put it together

Put it together: Mar comes straight from Old English merran, 'to spoil or hinder' — no prefix or suffix, just one very old root meaning to damage something's appearance.

Where it comes from

Where it comes from: Mar comes whole from Old English merran, 'to spoil or hinder' -- there is no prefix or suffix to peel off, just one compact, very old root. And watch out: 'marred' is not a new word built on this root; it is simply mar itself in the past tense.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Mar usually names a flaw or blemish spoiling an otherwise good thing (a scandal marred her reputation, a scratch marred the paint) — it's milder than 'ruin' or 'destroy,' pointing to a partial, not total, spoiling.
